comparator.name: Forest and Nature Conservation (Bachelor Bos- en Natuurbeheer)
comparator.sourceNotes: The current handbook defines a 180-EC bachelor with a 120-EC common part, one 30-EC specialisation and 30 EC of open electives. Society and Policy is selected by the official-order tie-break. The common part is reconstructed with the Wageningen location-dependent courses, Statistics 1, Research Methodology for Human–Environment Interactions and the 12-EC WUR thesis; the specialisation uses its Wageningen economics choice and the first listed 6-EC restricted option.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The generic target has two equally formal specialisations, Society and Policy and Ecology and Conservation. Neither is clearly broader or less specialised, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected before considering UCR fit.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme combines ecological and societal study. The two current WUR specialisations independently support a deeper Ecology and Conservation route and a Society and Policy route. All three are coherent, mechanically feasible and substantively distinct, so production stops at the maximum.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both introduce the coupled ecological and societal foundations of environmental stewardship.
Both introduce biodiversity and its observation across organisms and habitats.
Both apply ecological evidence to conservation and management.
Both address environmental risk, adaptation and planning, although WUR is forest-management specific.
Both establish ecosystem structure and functioning as a basis for later conservation study.
Both examine water and environmental systems, though UCR focuses on adaptation in deltas.
Both provide advanced ecosystem-focused study; UCR uses marine systems rather than forest landscapes.
Both use field-informed interdisciplinary work; WUR has a dedicated forest and nature field course.
Both integrate evidence, stakeholders and governance approaches in sustainability practice.
Both develop spatial and Earth-system tools for environmental evidence.
Both establish Earth-system and landscape context for ecological study.
No selected ordinary UCR course is a sufficiently direct one-to-one counterpart to the full People's Contributions to Forest & Nature Conservation component.
No selected ordinary UCR course is a sufficiently direct one-to-one counterpart to the full Ecology of Communities, Ecosystems and Landscapes: Theory component.
Both establish social-science perspectives on people, institutions and place.
Both examine public action, participation and social change around environmental issues.
Both introduce political institutions and public governance.
Both provide economic reasoning relevant to environmental choices and resource use.
Both address contested public decisions; UCR approaches them through international law.
Both examine conflict and governance in collective decision-making.
Both study public communication around sustainability and responsible action.
Both provide research design and statistical-method foundations.
Both analyse institutions and decision processes relevant to environmental organisations.
Both develop advanced analysis of political strategy and institutional change.
Both provide mathematical tools used in environmental analysis.
Both provide probability and statistical analysis for empirical research.
Both provide a quantitative foundation, with UCR oriented toward data analysis.
No selected ordinary UCR course is a sufficiently direct one-to-one counterpart to the full Ecology of Communities, Ecosystems and Landscapes: Field Excursions component.
No selected ordinary UCR course is a sufficiently direct one-to-one counterpart to the full BSc Thesis Forest and Nature Conservation component.
No selected ordinary UCR course is a sufficiently direct one-to-one counterpart to the full Open elective space component.

notes.text: WUR requires dedicated forest ecology, management planning, fieldwork and a 12-EC thesis within a 120-EC common core. UCR can combine ecology, environmental systems and governance into three defensible liberal-arts programmes, but it does not reproduce specialist forestry training or the same compulsory field and thesis structure.
